<result># Research Brief: SSE/FastAPI, uv Workflows, vcrpy+httpx Streaming (Sept 2026)

## A. Server-Sent Events: `sse-starlette` vs plain `StreamingResponse`

**What `EventSourceResponse` gives you beyond `StreamingResponse(media_type="text/event-stream")`:**
- **Keepalive pings**: built-in `ping` parameter (default 15s) spawns an asyncio task that interleaves `:`-comment frames to defeat proxy/LB idle timeouts (~60s on many LBs/nginx). Configurable via `ping_message_factory`; disable with `ping=0`. Plain `StreamingResponse` has none of this — you'd hand-roll it.
- **Disconnect detection**: runs a background task on `request.is_disconnected()` and cancels the generator task on client disconnect (raises `CancelledError` so your `try/finally` cleanup runs). With raw `StreamingResponse` you must poll `request.is_disconnected()` yourself inside the generator loop, or the generator keeps running/producing after the client is gone.
- **Graceful shutdown**: optional `shutdown_event` parameter lets generators receive a shutdown signal, emit a farewell event, and exit cleanly within a `shutdown_grace_period` before force-cancellation (avoids `CancelledError` noise on app shutdown / new deploys). This is app-lifecycle plumbing `StreamingResponse` doesn't provide (historically exposed via a module-level `AppStatus` in older sse-starlette versions, now via the `shutdown_event` mechanism).
- **Correct headers by default**: sets `Cache-Control: no-cache`, `Content-Type: text/event-stream`, and `X-Accel-Buffering: no`. With `StreamingResponse` you must set these three yourself or nginx/other proxies will buffer/cache the stream.
- Also gives typed `ServerSentEvent` objects (proper `data:`/`event:`/`id:`/`retry:` framing, including multi-line `data:` splitting) instead of you hand-formatting strings.

Current version: **sse-starlette 3.4.11** (released 2026-09-05), requires Python ≥3.10 (3.10–3.13), classified Production/Stable, actively maintained by sysid ([PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/sse-starlette/), [GitHub](https://github.com/sysid/sse-starlette)). FastAPI itself now documents SSE with a reference page pointing at `sse_starlette` types ([fastapi.tiangolo.com/reference/sse](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/reference/sse/), [fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/server-sent-events](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/server-sent-events/)).

**Pitfalls:**
- **Proxy buffering**: nginx, AWS ALB, and Cloudflare buffer responses by default — the most common production failure (events arrive in bursts or not until connection close). Fix requires *both* the `X-Accel-Buffering: no` header *and* `proxy_buffering off; proxy_read_timeout 3600s;` in the nginx location block — belt-and-suspenders, since some nginx versions ignore the header alone. Cloudflare additionally buffers ~100KB before flushing. HAProxy timeouts must exceed your heartbeat interval.
- **Browser `EventSource` can't POST** — it's GET-only and can't set custom headers (no Authorization header). For a POST-a-question-and-stream UX you must either (a) GET with the question in query params, or (b) use `fetch()` + manually read a `ReadableStream`, splitting on `\n\n` and parsing `data:`/`event:` lines yourself (~20 lines of code, well-trodden pattern).
- **`EventSource` auto-reconnect is a problem for agent runs**: native `EventSource` silently reconnects on drop and resends `Last-Event-ID`, but if your backend doesn't implement resume-from-last-event-id, naive servers just restart the whole agent/LLM run from scratch on reconnect — duplicate output and a duplicate (billed) LLM call. This is exactly why most people building agent-run streaming either (a) use `fetch()`+manual parsing (no auto-reconnect to worry about) or (b) explicitly support `Last-Event-ID` and a resumable cursor. For a one-day take-home, simplest is to *not* use native `EventSource` at all — avoids this whole class of bug.
- **SSE framing rules**: multi-line `data:` fields are joined with `\n` and only fire on the blank-line boundary; `retry:` sets client reconnect delay in ms (integer only); lines starting with `:` are comments (used for keepalive, ignored by clients); a line with no colon is a field name with empty value.
- Uvicorn itself has no special SSE handling — streaming just works via ASGI, but running behind a reverse proxy (not uvicorn directly) is where buffering issues appear.

**Recommendation for a one-day project with vanilla JS:** POST the question to a normal FastAPI endpoint that returns `EventSourceResponse` (or a raw `StreamingResponse` with the three headers set manually, if you want zero extra dependency), and on the frontend use `fetch()` + `ReadableStream` with a small hand-rolled `data:` parser (do **not** use the native `EventSource` object, since it can't POST and its auto-reconnect creates the duplicate-run hazard above). This is the least-machinery path that avoids GET-with-query-params awkwardness and avoids reconnect semantics you'd have to explicitly defeat.

## B. `uv` (Astral) lockfiles and workflows (2026)

**Core commands:**
- `uv lock` — explicitly (re)generates `uv.lock` from `pyproject.toml`.
- `uv sync --locked` — installs from the lock file but first **asserts the lock is up-to-date** with `pyproject.toml`; fails loudly on drift.
- `uv sync --frozen` — installs exactly what `uv.lock` pins, **never checks** it against `pyproject.toml` (a stale/drifted lock is silently used). Preferred in Docker builds where you want byte-for-byte reproducibility and don't want a lock-check to fail the build ([issue #16200](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/16200) documents `--frozen` being required in some container setups where `--locked` fails spuriously).
- `uv run <cmd>` — locks and syncs the project automatically before running (uses "inexact" sync: installs what's needed, doesn't remove extras); this auto-lock/auto-sync happens on every invocation unless you pass `--frozen`/`--no-sync`.

**Exporting a pinned `requirements.txt` from `uv.lock`:**
```
uv export --format requirements-txt --no-emit-project --no-hashes -o requirements.txt
```
Documented flags (from `uv export --help` / CLI reference):
- `--no-hashes` — exclude hashes (needed if the consumer can't parse pip's hash-pinned format).
- `--no-emit-project` — excludes the project's own `-e .` editable line.
- `--no-dev` / `--only-dev` — exclude/include the dev dependency group.
- `--group <name>`, `--no-group <name>`, `--only-group <name>` — arbitrary PEP 735 dependency groups.
- `--extra <name>` / `--all-extras` / `--no-extra <name>` — optional extras.
- `--package <name>` — **export only the subset needed by one workspace member** (answers your workspace-subset question directly — yes, this is supported, one package per invocation; can't pass `--package` multiple times in one call per a currently-open limitation).
- `--all-packages` — export the union across all workspace members.
- Astral's own guidance: prefer keeping `uv.lock` as source of truth and treat `requirements.txt` export as an interop/compat step for tools that require it — "we recommend against using both."

**Python version pinning:**
- `.python-version` file pins the *dev interpreter* uv will use/create the venv with; `uv python pin 3.12` writes/updates it.
- `requires-python` in `pyproject.toml` declares the *supported range* (e.g. `>=3.11`); the pinned `.python-version` must satisfy it or uv errors.
- By default uv auto-downloads a matching Python version as needed (no `uv python install` required), but `uv python install 3.12` explicitly fetches/installs one ahead of time.

**Bootstrap without preinstalled Python or uv:** uv does **not** require Python to bootstrap itself — the standalone installer (`curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh`) installs a static uv binary, after which `uv run script.py` works on a completely bare machine, uv fetching Python itself. This makes a Makefile target like `command -v uv || curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh` a legitimate one-day-project bootstrap — no separate Python/pip prerequisite.

**Workspaces (`[tool.uv.workspace]`)** — for a repo with `platform/` + `agent/` packages: uv workspaces (Cargo/npm-workspace-style) give you one shared `uv.lock` and one venv across both packages, with local packages installed editable so cross-package edits are picked up instantly, and CI installs guaranteed to match what devs run locally. Configured via root `pyproject.toml`'s `[tool.uv.workspace]` with `members`/`exclude`. For a **one-day take-home** with just two small packages, this is arguably more machinery than needed — a **flat single-root project** (one `pyproject.toml`, `agent/` and `platform/` as plain subpackages or a `src/` layout with local path dependencies) is simpler to set up and explain, and avoids workspace-specific gotchas people report (e.g., needing `--package` to scope commands, editable-install surprises). Workspaces earn their cost when packages are independently versioned/published or the repo is expected to grow — worth mentioning as the "if this grows" answer, but not the one-day default.

Sources: [uv Locking and syncing docs](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/sync/), [uv Exporting a lockfile docs](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/export/), [uv CLI reference](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/cli/), [uv Python versions docs](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/python-versions/), [uv Installation docs](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/), [Have `uv sync` default to `--locked` #12372](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/12372), [Frozen vs Locked unexpected behavior #9379](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/9379), [uv sync requires --frozen in Docker #16200](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/16200), [pydevtools: export requirements.txt](https://pydevtools.com/handbook/how-to/how-to-export-requirements-txt-from-a-uv-project/), [pydevtools: monorepo with uv workspaces](https://pydevtools.com/handbook/how-to/how-to-set-up-a-python-monorepo-with-uv-workspaces/), [Workspaces with subset of packages #9571](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/9571).

## C. `pytest-recording`/`vcrpy` + `httpx` + OpenAI streaming — is it a trap?

**Verdict up front: yes, treat streaming cassettes as a trap for a one-day project.** vcrpy's httpx support is real and improving, but streaming replay is architecturally fragile and has open, unresolved bugs as of 2026. Non-streaming (buffered JSON) OpenAI calls are fine to record/replay; streaming SSE calls are not something to bet a one-day take-home's test suite on.

**httpx support status:** vcrpy currently ships **8.3.0** (released 2026-07-04). httpx support was **rewritten in 8.3.0 to patch `httpcore` instead of `httpx` directly**, specifically to fix `httpx.ResponseNotRead` exceptions (issues #832/#834/#943). 8.2.0 separately fixed sync-requests-in-async-context bugs (#965). So sync and async httpx are both nominally supported, but the implementation has been churning recently — a sign it's not fully settled.

**Streaming — the crux, with concrete evidence it's fragile:**
- [vcrpy #597](https://github.com/kevin1024/vcrpy/issues/597) "async httpx streaming doesn't work" — root cause was httpx's `stream()` calling `send()` with only kwargs while vcrpy's stub expected positional args (`IndexError` at `vcr/stubs/httpx_stubs.py:72`). Closed, but shows the stub layer has historically been out of sync with httpx's internal calling conventions — exactly the kind of thing that breaks again on httpx/vcrpy version bumps.
- [vcrpy #927](https://github.com/kevin1024/vcrpy/issues/927), **open as of July 2025**: google-genai (streaming, via aiohttp) hits an **infinite loop replaying from a cassette** because vcrpy's `MockStream` returns a fresh instance on every access of `.content`, so a `while True: readline()` loop never advances past the first line — it's not a proper stream cursor. This is a structural problem with how vcrpy models streamed bodies, not a one-off bug, and the maintainers note it "breaks any code using stateful iteration patterns — increasingly common in modern async libraries and AI tools." No fix merged yet.
- httpx itself has a related, separate wrinkle: `iter_bytes(chunk_size=...)` can drop the last partial chunk ([httpx #394](https://github.com/encode/httpx/issues/394), [discussion #3543](https://github.com/encode/httpx/discussions/3543)) — not vcrpy's bug, but compounds risk if your streaming code path relies on `iter_bytes`.
- General pattern across these issues: vcrpy cassettes are fundamentally built around a "response body as one buffered artifact" model. It can capture and store chunked/streamed bodies, but faithfully replaying them so client code that does *stateful* incremental reads (readline loops, `aiter_lines`, etc.) sees the same chunk-by-chunk behavior as the live network response is exactly where it breaks. Real-time timing (how long between chunks) is not preserved at all — cassette replay is effectively instantaneous, which is fine for correctness tests but means you can't test streaming *latency/backpressure* behavior against a cassette.
- I could not find a definitive, current (2026) success story of someone reliably recording+replaying **OpenAI SDK streaming (`stream=True`)** specifically through vcrpy/pytest-recording; what I found instead were either non-streaming OpenAI cassette examples, or open bug reports about streaming replay breaking for adjacent LLM SDKs (google-genai) hitting the same vcrpy stream-modeling limitation. Given the OpenAI Python SDK itself is httpx-based, it's plausible it hits similar issues.

**Alternatives people actually use for testing streaming LLM clients:**
- **`respx`** (httpx-native mock library) — intercepts httpx requests and lets you return a canned `httpx.Response` with a custom streaming body/iterator you construct yourself, giving full control over chunk boundaries — this is the most commonly recommended approach specifically because you author the SSE chunks by hand rather than trusting a recorder to capture them faithfully. There's a purpose-built plugin, `openai-responses` (pytest plugin, "powered by respx"), which added **streaming response support in v0.4**, purpose-built for OpenAI SDK testing.
- **`pytest-httpx`** — similar httpx-mock-based approach, full manual control.
- **Hand-written fake clients / fake-model hooks** — many agent frameworks recommend a fake/stub LLM client (returning a scripted async generator of chunks) over any HTTP-layer recording, specifically to sidestep this whole class of streaming-replay bug.

**Recommendation for a one-day take-home:** use `respx` (or a hand-rolled fake client) for anything that streams from OpenAI — you write the exact SSE chunk sequence, so it's deterministic, fast, and doesn't depend on vcrpy internals that are actively churning. Reserve vcrpy/pytest-recording (if you use it at all) for **non-streaming** calls, where it's mature and low-risk.

**Scrubbing the API key / record modes (mechanics, in case you do use vcrpy for non-streaming calls):**
- `filter_headers=[("authorization", "REDACTED")]` (or `["authorization"]` to just drop the value) passed to `vcr_config`/`use_cassette` — a list of `(header, replacement)` tuples; replacement can be a string, `None` to remove the header/value entirely, or a callable `(key, value, request) -> str | None`.
- `record_mode` options: **`none`** (replay only, error on any new request — pytest-recording's default, to prevent accidental live calls in CI), **`once`** (replay if cassette exists, record if it doesn't, error on new requests if cassette exists — vcrpy's own default), **`new_episodes`** (always allowed to record new interactions in addition to replaying existing ones), **`all`** (vcrpy's name — always records, never replays; useful for full re-recording). **`rewrite`** is a **pytest-recording-specific** addition (since v0.7.0) that deletes the existing cassette file first, then records fresh — not a native vcrpy mode.

Sources: [vcrpy Releases](https://github.com/kevin1024/vcrpy/releases), [vcrpy Changelog](https://vcrpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/changelog.html), [vcrpy #597](https://github.com/kevin1024/vcrpy/issues/597), [vcrpy #927](https://github.com/kevin1024/vcrpy/issues/927), [vcrpy #895](https://github.com/kevin1024/vcrpy/issues/895), [httpx #394](https://github.com/encode/httpx/issues/394), [httpx discussion #3543](https://github.com/encode/httpx/discussions/3543), [vcrpy Usage docs (record modes)](https://vcrpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/usage.html), [Simon Willison TIL: pytest-recording + VCR](https://til.simonwillison.net/pytest/pytest-recording-vcr), [pytest-recording repo](https://github.com/kiwicom/pytest-recording), [Redacting secrets from VCR.py cassettes](https://imoskvin.com/blog/redacting-vcrpy-cassettes/), [respx](https://lundberg.github.io/respx/), [openai-responses (respx-based pytest plugin, streaming since v0.4)](https://github.com/mharrisb1/openai-responses-python), [Mocking OpenAI - unit testing in the age of LLMs](https://laszlo.substack.com/p/mocking-openai-unit-testing-in-the), [Shades of testing HTTP requests in Python](https://rednafi.com/python/testing_http_requests/).</result>

## 1. `Runner.run_streamed(...)`

**Not async. Not awaited.** It is a plain `@classmethod` that returns immediately (`src/agents/run.py:468-483`):

```python
class Runner:
    @classmethod
    def run_streamed(
        cls,
        starting_agent: Agent[TContext],
        input: str | list[TResponseInputItem] | RunState[TContext],
        context: TContext | None = None,
        max_turns: int | None = DEFAULT_MAX_TURNS,
        hooks: RunHooks[TContext] | None = None,
        run_config: RunConfig | dict[str, Any] | None = None,
        previous_response_id: str | None = None,
        auto_previous_response_id: bool = False,
        conversation_id: str | None = None,
        session: Session | None = None,
        *,
        error_handlers: RunErrorHandlers[TContext] | None = None,
    ) -> RunResultStreaming:
```

Gotcha worth noting: in `run_streamed` the `*` marker sits at the **end** (only `error_handlers` is kw-only), so `context`/`max_turns`/etc. are positional-or-keyword. ```python
result = Runner.run_streamed(agent, input="Please tell me 5 jokes.")
async for event in result.stream_events():
    ...

The docs are explicit (`docs/streaming.md:7`): *"Keep consuming `result.stream_events()` until the async iterator finishes. A streaming run is not complete until the iterator ends"* — session persistence, approval bookkeeping and history compaction can finish after the last visible token.

## 3. Raw response deltas

`run_internal/run_loop.py:2286` wraps **every** chunk from the model stream verbatim:

```python
async for event in model_events:
    streamed_result._event_queue.put_nowait(RawResponsesStreamEvent(data=event))
```

and `models/openai_responses.py:697-754` `yield chunk`s every SSE chunk unmodified. So the full `openai.types.responses.ResponseStreamEvent` union reaches you.

**Text deltas** — `ResponseTextDeltaEvent`, `type == "response.output_text.delta"`, field `.delta: str` (plus `content_index`, `item_id`, `output_index`, `sequence_number`, `logprobs`). Official detection idiom (`docs/streaming.md:30-31`):

```python
from openai.types.responses import ResponseTextDeltaEvent

async for event in result.stream_events():
    if event.type == "raw_response_event" and isinstance(event.data, ResponseTextDeltaEvent):
        print(event.data.delta, end="", flush=True)
```

**Tool-call ARGUMENT deltas** — yes, available. `ResponseFunctionCallArgumentsDeltaEvent`, `type == "response.function_call_arguments.delta"`, fields `.delta: str` (*"The function-call arguments delta that is added"*), `.item_id: str`, `.output_index: int`, `.sequence_number: int`. There is a matching `ResponseFunctionCallArgumentsDoneEvent`. Note the delta event carries **no tool name** — pair it with `ResponseOutputItemAddedEvent` (`type == "response.output_item.added"`, `.item`, `.output_index`) to learn the name for a given `item_id`/`output_index`:

```python
from openai.types.responses import (
    ResponseOutputItemAddedEvent,
    ResponseFunctionCallArgumentsDeltaEvent,
    ResponseFunctionToolCall,
)

names: dict[str, str] = {}   # item_id -> tool name
buf: dict[str, str] = {}     # item_id -> accumulated JSON

async for event in result.stream_events():
    if event.type != "raw_response_event":
        continue
    d = event.data
    if isinstance(d, ResponseOutputItemAddedEvent) and isinstance(d.item, ResponseFunctionToolCall):
        names[d.item.id or d.item.call_id] = d.item.name
    elif isinstance(d, ResponseFunctionCallArgumentsDeltaEvent):
        buf[d.item_id] = buf.get(d.item_id, "") + d.delta
        print(names.get(d.item_id, "?"), d.delta)
```

Related delta events in the same union, if you need them: `ResponseReasoningTextDeltaEvent`, `ResponseReasoningSummaryTextDeltaEvent`, `ResponseRefusalDeltaEvent`, `ResponseMcpCallArgumentsDeltaEvent`, `ResponseCustomToolCallInputDeltaEvent`, `ResponseCodeInterpreterCallCodeDeltaEvent`, `ResponseShellCallCommandDeltaEvent`, `ResponseShellCallOutputContentDeltaEvent`, `ResponseAudioDeltaEvent`, `ResponseAudioTranscriptDeltaEvent`.

⚠️ **Flag:** the OpenAI event class/field details come from `openai-python` **main**, not a tag pinned to whatever `openai` version 0.22.2 resolves to. The two core ones (`response.output_text.delta`, `response.function_call_arguments.delta`) are long-stable and one of them is quoted directly in the SDK's own 0.22.2 docs, so I'm confident about those; the more exotic delta events at the tail of that list are lower-confidence for this exact pin.

### ✅ Confirmation: which exist on the STREAMING result, and when they're populated

Every `RunResultBase` member above — `final_output`, `final_output_as`, `new_items`, `raw_responses`, `last_agent`, `input_guardrail_results`, `output_guardrail_results`, `to_input_list()`, `context_wrapper`, `last_response_id` — **exists on `RunResultStreaming`** by inheritance.

Population timing, from the construction site (`run.py:2532-2577`) and the run loop:

- **Available immediately, before you consume anything:** `context_wrapper` (passed into the constructor), `max_turns`, `trace`, `current_agent`. `result.context_wrapper.context` is your object from the first line.
- **Initialized empty/None at construction, filled during the stream:** `final_output=None`, `is_complete=False`, `new_items=[]`, `raw_responses=[]`, `interruptions=[]`, `current_turn=0`, guardrail-result lists `[]`. (When resuming from a `RunState`, these are seeded from the state instead.)
- **`current_agent`** updates live as handoffs occur — `docs/results.md:117` says so explicitly, so you can observe handoffs mid-stream. `last_agent` is only *true*-final once complete.
- **`final_output` is `None` until the stream finishes** (`docs/results.md:39`, and the field docstring: *"This is None until the agent has finished running"*). In `run_internal/run_loop.py:653-658` it's assigned, then `is_complete = True`, then the `QueueCompleteSentinel` is queued — so by the time your `async for` exits normally, `final_output` is set.
- **`raw_responses` / `last_response_id` / `new_items` / guardrail lists** accumulate progressively and are only complete at iterator end.
- **`context_wrapper.usage`** lags — the `RunContextWrapper.usage` docstring says *"For streamed responses, the usage will be stale until the last chunk of the stream is processed."*
- Rule of thumb, straight from `docs/results.md:197`: summary properties *"may still be settling after the last visible token arrives."* Read them after the loop exits, not inside it.

Python-specific absence worth flagging (`docs/results.md:201`): unlike the JS SDK there is **no** streamed `completed` promise and **no** `.error` property. Also no `.output` property — use `new_items` or `raw_responses`.

All inherit `RunItemBase` (`items.py:97-153`), which gives every run item:

- `.raw_item: T`
- `.to_input_item() -> TResponseInputItem`
- `.release_agent()`

```python

class MessageOutputItem(RunItemBase[ResponseOutputMessage]):
    raw_item: ResponseOutputMessage
    type: Literal["message_output_item"] = "message_output_item"
```

```python
@dataclass

    raw_item: ToolCallItemTypes
    type: Literal["tool_call_item"] = "tool_call_item"
    description: str | None = None
    title: str | None = None
    tool_origin: ToolOrigin | None = None
    _resolved_tool_name: str | None = field(default=None, kw_only=True, repr=False)

    @property
    def tool_name(self) -> str | None: ...   # NOTE: property, added in recent versions

```

`ToolCallItemTypes = ResponseFunctionToolCall | ResponseComputerToolCall | ResponseFileSearchToolCall | ResponseFunctionWebSearch | McpCall | ResponseCodeInterpreterToolCall | ImageGenerationCall | LocalShellCall | Program | dict[str, Any]`

```python
@dataclass

    raw_item: ToolCallOutputTypes
    output: Any          # ← the actual return value of the tool
    type: Literal["tool_call_output_item"] = "tool_call_output_item"

### How to extract name / args / output

- **Tool NAME:** use the `ToolCallItem.tool_name` property — it is mapping-safe and falls back to the SDK-resolved name. Do **not** hand-roll `item.raw_item.name`; many raw items are plain `dict`s (`ToolCallItemTypes` includes `dict[str, Any]`, and `docs/results.md:87` warns that program-owned shell/apply-patch calls use mappings).
- **Tool ARGUMENTS:** there is **no `.arguments` property on `ToolCallItem`** (only `ToolApprovalItem` has one, at `items.py:645`). Read it off the raw item: for `ResponseFunctionToolCall` it is `arguments: str` — *"A JSON string of the arguments to pass to the function."* Use a mapping-safe getter.
- **Tool OUTPUT:** `ToolCallOutputItem.output` — the real Python return value. The field docstring: *"This is whatever the tool call returned; the `raw_item` contains a string representation of the output."* So `.output` for the value, `raw_item["output"]` for the stringified form.
- **Message TEXT:** `ItemHelpers.text_message_output(item) -> str` (concatenates `ResponseOutputText` parts of `raw_item.content`), or `ItemHelpers.text_message_outputs(items)` across a list.

### Working sketch over `result.new_items`

```python
import json
from collections.abc import Mapping

from agents import (
    Agent, ItemHelpers, MessageOutputItem, Runner,
    ToolCallItem, ToolCallOutputItem,
)


def raw_field(item, name):
    """Mapping-safe raw_item accessor (the pattern the official docs recommend)."""
    raw = item.raw_item
    if isinstance(raw, Mapping):
        return raw.get(name)
    return getattr(raw, name, None)


result = await Runner.run(agent, "What's the weather in Tokyo?")

for item in result.new_items:
    if isinstance(item, ToolCallItem):
        args_json = raw_field(item, "arguments")          # JSON string, or None
        try:
            args = json.loads(args_json) if args_json else {}
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            args = args_json
        print(f"[call]   name={item.tool_name} call_id={item.call_id} args={args}")

    elif isinstance(item, ToolCallOutputItem):
        print(f"[output] call_id={item.call_id} output={item.output!r}")

    elif isinstance(item, MessageOutputItem):
        print(f"[message] {ItemHelpers.text_message_output(item)}")
```

### ✅ EXPLICIT CONFIRMATION: local context is NOT sent to the LLM

Two independent primary sources say so.

The class docstring in `src/agents/run_context.py:73-78`:

> **NOTE: Contexts are not passed to the LLM.** They're a way to pass dependencies and data to code you implement, like tool functions, callbacks, hooks, etc.

And `docs/context.md:26-28`, in a `!!! danger` admonition:

> The context object is **not** sent to the LLM. It is purely a local object that you can read from, write to and call methods on it.

Reinforced by `docs/context.md:151`: *"When an LLM is called, the **only** data it can see is from the conversation history."* To get data to the model you must put it in `instructions`, in `input`, behind a `FunctionTool`, or via retrieval/web search.

### Passing and reading it

```python
import asyncio
from dataclasses import dataclass

from agents import Agent, RunContextWrapper, Runner
from agents.decorators import tool          # `tool` is an alias: decorators.py line 10 is `tool = function_tool`

@dataclass
class UserInfo:
    name: str
    uid: int

@tool
async def fetch_user_age(wrapper: RunContextWrapper[UserInfo]) -> str:
    """Fetch the age of the user."""
    return f"The user {wrapper.context.name} is 47 years old"

async def main():
    user_info = UserInfo(name="John", uid=123)
    agent = Agent[UserInfo](name="Assistant", tools=[fetch_user_age])
    result = await Runner.run(agent, "What is the age of the user?", context=user_info)
    print(result.final_output)
```

- The tool's **first parameter** is typed `RunContextWrapper[T]` (or the `ToolContext[T]` subclass); the SDK injects it and it is *not* exposed to the model as a JSON-schema parameter.
- Parametrize the agent as `Agent[UserInfo]` so the typechecker catches mismatches. `docs/context.md:18`: *"every agent, tool function, lifecycle etc for a given agent run must use the same type of context."*

### Reading it after the run — **both work**

`result.context_wrapper` **is** available (it's a `RunResultBase` field, on `RunResult` and `RunResultStreaming` alike), and `result.context_wrapper.context` is the **same object** you passed — `ensure_context_wrapper` (`run_internal/agent_runner_helpers.py:357-363`) does `RunContextWrapper(context=context)` with no copy:

```python
def ensure_context_wrapper(context):
    if isinstance(context, RunContextWrapper):
        return context
    return RunContextWrapper(context=cast(TContext, context))
```

So mutations your tools made are visible both through your own reference and through `result.context_wrapper.context`. You may also pass a pre-built `RunContextWrapper` as `context=` and it is reused by identity.

Use `result.context_wrapper` when you also want SDK runtime metadata — `.usage`, approval state, `.tool_input` (`docs/results.md:228`). Persistence caveat from `docs/context.md:53`: that runtime metadata is saved into a serialized `RunState`, so **don't put secrets in `.context`** if you intend to persist or transmit state.

`ToolContext[T]` (subclass, `agents.tool_context.ToolContext`) additionally exposes `tool_name`, `tool_call_id`, `tool_arguments`, `tool_namespace`, `qualified_tool_name`.

## 7. Streaming gotchas

### Output guardrail tripwire mid-stream

**Exception:** `OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered` (exported from `agents`). **When:** output guardrails run only once the turn reaches `NextStepFinalOutput` — `run.py:1913-1930` shows `await run_output_guardrails(...)` inside `if isinstance(turn_result.next_step, NextStepFinalOutput)`. That is **after** the final message tokens have already been emitted as raw deltas.

**This is the big trap:** you will have already streamed the offending text to your user before the tripwire fires. If you stream raw text deltas straight to a UI, buffer or use a "commit on completion" pattern.

Propagation path: the exception escapes `run_loop_task` → `_check_errors()` (`result.py:1128-1138`) stores it in `_stored_exception` → `stream_events()` raises it at `result.py:1076-1085`, after the `finally` block has drained queues and run cleanup. `docs/guardrails.md:54` confirms: *"Streaming runs use the same persistence ordering as non-streaming runs and raise the terminal exception from `stream_events()`."*

Redaction note (`docs/results.md:224`): when an output guardrail blocks output that came directly from a terminal function tool, `output_guardrail_results` and `tool_output_guardrail_results` are **sanitized** — payloads replaced with `"Output withheld by an output guardrail."`. The sanitized result is on `exc.guardrail_result`.

### Cancellation — yes, `.cancel()` exists

```python
def cancel(self, mode: Literal["immediate", "after_turn"] = "immediate") -> None:
```

(`result.py:878`.) Two modes:
- `"immediate"` (default) — `_cleanup_tasks()` cancels `run_loop_task`, the sandbox-wrapped loop, and both guardrail tasks; sets `is_complete = True`; clears the input-guardrail queue; pushes a `QueueCompleteSentinel` to unblock waiting consumers.
- `"after_turn"` — sets `_cancel_mode` only and returns; the loop stops before the next turn begins. Per the docstring: lets the LLM response finish, executes pending tool calls, saves session state properly, tracks usage accurately.

**Critical:** the docstring says *"After calling cancel(), you should continue consuming stream_events() to allow the cancellation to complete properly."* `docs/results.md:199` repeats this. Breaking out of the `async for` without draining leaves cleanup unfinished.

Also, if the *consuming task itself* is cancelled while awaiting the queue, `stream_events()` catches `asyncio.CancelledError`, calls `self.cancel()`, and re-raises (`result.py:1019-1022`).

### Do exceptions surface from `stream_events()`?

**Yes** — that is the designed channel. The `RunResultStreaming` class docstring: *"The streaming method will raise: A `MaxTurnsExceeded` exception if the agent exceeds the max_turns limit; A tripwire exception if a guardrail is tripped, e.g. `InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered` or `OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered`."* `_check_errors()` also captures failures from `run_loop_task` and `_input_guardrails_task`. Exceptions are raised **after** the generator's `finally` (cleanup, queue drain), so the exception arrives once the run has settled.

**One documented escape hatch / edge case.** A run-loop failure that happens *before* any stream event is produced (the docstring's example: early sandbox initialisation) may not be re-raised through `stream_events()`. Hence `run_loop_exception`, with this exact recipe in its docstring (`result.py:850-876`):

```python
result = Runner.run_streamed(agent, "hello")
async for event in result.stream_events():
    pass
if result.run_loop_exception:
    raise result.run_loop_exception
```

It returns `None` if the loop succeeded, hasn't finished, or was cancelled.

### Other streaming gotchas worth knowing

- **Approvals end the stream early.** If a tool needs approval, `stream_events()` simply *finishes* — no exception. Check `result.interruptions`, then `state = result.to_state()`, `state.approve(interruption)`, and re-run `Runner.run_streamed(agent, state)`. Don't mistake a clean exit for a completed run; check `result.interruptions`.
- **Cancelling during an output guardrail:** `docs/guardrails.md:54` — an immediate `cancel()` while the output guardrail is running cancels the in-flight guardrail and does **not** start a final-turn session write.
- **After `cancel(mode="after_turn")` stopped on a tool turn**, rerun `result.last_agent` with `result.to_input_list(mode="normalized")` to continue the unfinished user turn rather than appending a fresh one (`docs/streaming.md:64`).

## 1. Streaming

`Runner.run_streamed(agent, input=...)` returns a `RunResultStreaming` immediately (no await). Iterate with:
```python
result = Runner.run_streamed(agent, input="...")
async for event in result.stream_events():
    ...
```
`StreamEvent` is a union of three types (`agents/stream_events.py`):

- **`RawResponsesStreamEvent`**: `type: Literal["raw_response_event"]`, `data: TResponseStreamEvent` — raw OpenAI Responses API events passed straight through. **Text deltas**: check `event.type == "raw_response_event" and isinstance(event.data, ResponseTextDeltaEvent)` (from `openai.types.responses`), then read `event.data.delta`.
- **`RunItemStreamEvent`**: `type: Literal["run_item_stream_event"]`, `name: Literal[...]`, `item: RunItem`. Exact `name` values (confirmed in source): `message_output_created`, `handoff_requested`, `handoff_occured` (sic — intentional misspelling kept for back-compat), `tool_called`, `tool_search_called`, `tool_search_output_created`, `tool_output`, `reasoning_item_created`, `mcp_approval_requested`, `mcp_approval_response`, `mcp_list_tools`.
- **`AgentUpdatedStreamEvent`**: `type: Literal["agent_updated_stream_event"]`, `new_agent: Agent[Any]`.

RunItem subclasses (`agents/items.py`) have their own `.type` field distinct from the event `name`: `ToolCallItem.type == "tool_call_item"`, `ToolCallOutputItem.type == "tool_call_output_item"`, `MessageOutputItem.type == "message_output_item"`.

**Tool name/arguments from a `tool_called` event**: `event.item` is a `ToolCallItem` with `raw_item: ToolCallItemTypes`. For a function tool, `raw_item` is `ResponseFunctionToolCall`, so: `event.item.raw_item.name` (str) and `json.loads(event.item.raw_item.arguments)` (arguments arrive as a JSON-encoded string). Tool output: `event.item.output` on the `ToolCallOutputItem`.

## 2. Fake/scripted model for tests

The `Model`/`ModelProvider` protocol lives in `agents/models/interface.py`:
```python
class Model(abc.ABC):
    @abc.abstractmethod
    async def get_response(
        self, system_instructions, input, model_settings, tools,
        output_schema, handoffs, tracing, *,
        previous_response_id, conversation_id, prompt,
    ) -> ModelResponse: ...

    @abc.abstractmethod
    def stream_response(
        self, system_instructions, input, model_settings, tools,
        output_schema, handoffs, tracing, *,
        previous_response_id, conversation_id, prompt,
    ) -> AsyncIterator[TResponseStreamEvent]: ...

class ModelProvider(abc.ABC):
    @abc.abstractmethod
    def get_model(self, model_name: str | None) -> Model: ...
```

    def run_streamed(
        cls,
        starting_agent: Agent[TContext],
        input: str | list[TResponseInputItem] | RunState[TContext],
        context: TContext | None = None,
        max_turns: int | None = DEFAULT_MAX_TURNS,

Contrast `Runner.run` (`run.py:261-275`), where `*` comes right after `input` so **everything** including `context` is kw-only, and it **is** `async def ... -> RunResult`.

Consumption is `async for` over `stream_events()`, which is `async def stream_events(self) -> AsyncIterator[StreamEvent]` (`result.py:942`):

```python

async for event in result.stream_events():
    ...
```

The docs are explicit (`docs/streaming.md:7`): *"Keep consuming `result.stream_events()` until the async iterator finishes. A streaming run is not complete until the iterator ends"* — session persistence, approval bookkeeping and history compaction can finish after the last visible token.

## 3. Raw response deltas

`run_internal/run_loop.py:2286` wraps **every** chunk from the model stream verbatim:

```python
async for event in model_events:
    streamed_result._event_queue.put_nowait(RawResponsesStreamEvent(data=event))
```

and `models/openai_responses.py:697-754` `yield chunk`s every SSE chunk unmodified. So the full `openai.types.responses.ResponseStreamEvent` union reaches you.

**Text deltas** — `ResponseTextDeltaEvent`, `type == "response.output_text.delta"`, field `.delta: str` (plus `content_index`, `item_id`, `output_index`, `sequence_number`, `logprobs`). Official detection idiom (`docs/streaming.md:30-31`):

```python
from openai.types.responses import ResponseTextDeltaEvent

async for event in result.stream_events():
    if event.type == "raw_response_event" and isinstance(event.data, ResponseTextDeltaEvent):
        print(event.data.delta, end="", flush=True)
```

**Tool-call ARGUMENT deltas** — yes, available. `ResponseFunctionCallArgumentsDeltaEvent`, `type == "response.function_call_arguments.delta"`, fields `.delta: str` (*"The function-call arguments delta that is added"*), `.item_id: str`, `.output_index: int`, `.sequence_number: int`. There is a matching `ResponseFunctionCallArgumentsDoneEvent`. Note the delta event carries **no tool name** — pair it with `ResponseOutputItemAddedEvent` (`type == "response.output_item.added"`, `.item`, `.output_index`) to learn the name for a given `item_id`/`output_index`:

```python
from openai.types.responses import (
    ResponseOutputItemAddedEvent,
    ResponseFunctionCallArgumentsDeltaEvent,
    ResponseFunctionToolCall,
)

names: dict[str, str] = {}   # item_id -> tool name
buf: dict[str, str] = {}     # item_id -> accumulated JSON

async for event in result.stream_events():
    if event.type != "raw_response_event":
        continue
    d = event.data
    if isinstance(d, ResponseOutputItemAddedEvent) and isinstance(d.item, ResponseFunctionToolCall):
        names[d.item.id or d.item.call_id] = d.item.name
    elif isinstance(d, ResponseFunctionCallArgumentsDeltaEvent):
        buf[d.item_id] = buf.get(d.item_id, "") + d.delta
        print(names.get(d.item_id, "?"), d.delta)
```

Related delta events in the same union, if you need them: `ResponseReasoningTextDeltaEvent`, `ResponseReasoningSummaryTextDeltaEvent`, `ResponseRefusalDeltaEvent`, `ResponseMcpCallArgumentsDeltaEvent`, `ResponseCustomToolCallInputDeltaEvent`, `ResponseCodeInterpreterCallCodeDeltaEvent`, `ResponseShellCallCommandDeltaEvent`, `ResponseShellCallOutputContentDeltaEvent`, `ResponseAudioDeltaEvent`, `ResponseAudioTranscriptDeltaEvent`.

⚠️ **Flag:** the OpenAI event class/field details come from `openai-python` **main**, not a tag pinned to whatever `openai` version 0.22.2 resolves to. The two core ones (`response.output_text.delta`, `response.function_call_arguments.delta`) are long-stable and one of them is quoted directly in the SDK's own 0.22.2 docs, so I'm confident about those; the more exotic delta events at the tail of that list are lower-confidence for this exact pin.

Population timing, from the construction site (`run.py:2532-2577`) and the run loop:

- **Initialized empty/None at construction, filled during the stream:** `final_output=None`, `is_complete=False`, `new_items=[]`, `raw_responses=[]`, `interruptions=[]`, `current_turn=0`, guardrail-result lists `[]`. (When resuming from a `RunState`, these are seeded from the state instead.)

- **`final_output` is `None` until the stream finishes** (`docs/results.md:39`, and the field docstring: *"This is None until the agent has finished running"*). In `run_internal/run_loop.py:653-658` it's assigned, then `is_complete = True`, then the `QueueCompleteSentinel` is queued — so by the time your `async for` exits normally, `final_output` is set.
- **`raw_responses` / `last_response_id` / `new_items` / guardrail lists** accumulate progressively and are only complete at iterator end.
- **`context_wrapper.usage`** lags — the `RunContextWrapper.usage` docstring says *"For streamed responses, the usage will be stale until the last chunk of the stream is processed."*
- Rule of thumb, straight from `docs/results.md:197`: summary properties *"may still be settling after the last visible token arrives."* Read them after the loop exits, not inside it.

### How to extract name / args / output

- **Tool NAME:** use the `ToolCallItem.tool_name` property — it is mapping-safe and falls back to the SDK-resolved name. Do **not** hand-roll `item.raw_item.name`; many raw items are plain `dict`s (`ToolCallItemTypes` includes `dict[str, Any]`, and `docs/results.md:87` warns that program-owned shell/apply-patch calls use mappings).
- **Tool ARGUMENTS:** there is **no `.arguments` property on `ToolCallItem`** (only `ToolApprovalItem` has one, at `items.py:645`). Read it off the raw item: for `ResponseFunctionToolCall` it is `arguments: str` — *"A JSON string of the arguments to pass to the function."* Use a mapping-safe getter.
- **Tool OUTPUT:** `ToolCallOutputItem.output` — the real Python return value. The field docstring: *"This is whatever the tool call returned; the `raw_item` contains a string representation of the output."* So `.output` for the value, `raw_item["output"]` for the stringified form.
- **Message TEXT:** `ItemHelpers.text_message_output(item) -> str` (concatenates `ResponseOutputText` parts of `raw_item.content`), or `ItemHelpers.text_message_outputs(items)` across a list.

### Working sketch over `result.new_items`

import json
from collections.abc import Mapping

from agents import (
    Agent, ItemHelpers, MessageOutputItem, Runner,
    ToolCallItem, ToolCallOutputItem,
)


def raw_field(item, name):
    """Mapping-safe raw_item accessor (the pattern the official docs recommend)."""
    raw = item.raw_item
    if isinstance(raw, Mapping):
        return raw.get(name)
    return getattr(raw, name, None)


result = await Runner.run(agent, "What's the weather in Tokyo?")

for item in result.new_items:
    if isinstance(item, ToolCallItem):
        args_json = raw_field(item, "arguments")          # JSON string, or None
        try:
            args = json.loads(args_json) if args_json else {}
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            args = args_json
        print(f"[call]   name={item.tool_name} call_id={item.call_id} args={args}")

    elif isinstance(item, ToolCallOutputItem):
        print(f"[output] call_id={item.call_id} output={item.output!r}")

    elif isinstance(item, MessageOutputItem):
        print(f"[message] {ItemHelpers.text_message_output(item)}")

### ✅ EXPLICIT CONFIRMATION: local context is NOT sent to the LLM

Two independent primary sources say so.

The class docstring in `src/agents/run_context.py:73-78`:

> **NOTE: Contexts are not passed to the LLM.** They're a way to pass dependencies and data to code you implement, like tool functions, callbacks, hooks, etc.

And `docs/context.md:26-28`, in a `!!! danger` admonition:

> The context object is **not** sent to the LLM. It is purely a local object that you can read from, write to and call methods on it.

Reinforced by `docs/context.md:151`: *"When an LLM is called, the **only** data it can see is from the conversation history."* To get data to the model you must put it in `instructions`, in `input`, behind a `FunctionTool`, or via retrieval/web search.

### Passing and reading it

```python
import asyncio
from dataclasses import dataclass

from agents import Agent, RunContextWrapper, Runner
from agents.decorators import tool          # `tool` is an alias: decorators.py line 10 is `tool = function_tool`

@dataclass
class UserInfo:
    name: str
    uid: int

@tool
async def fetch_user_age(wrapper: RunContextWrapper[UserInfo]) -> str:
    """Fetch the age of the user."""
    return f"The user {wrapper.context.name} is 47 years old"

async def main():
    user_info = UserInfo(name="John", uid=123)
    agent = Agent[UserInfo](name="Assistant", tools=[fetch_user_age])
    result = await Runner.run(agent, "What is the age of the user?", context=user_info)
    print(result.final_output)
```

- The tool's **first parameter** is typed `RunContextWrapper[T]` (or the `ToolContext[T]` subclass); the SDK injects it and it is *not* exposed to the model as a JSON-schema parameter.
- Parametrize the agent as `Agent[UserInfo]` so the typechecker catches mismatches. `docs/context.md:18`: *"every agent, tool function, lifecycle etc for a given agent run must use the same type of context."*

### Reading it after the run — **both work**

`result.context_wrapper` **is** available (it's a `RunResultBase` field, on `RunResult` and `RunResultStreaming` alike), and `result.context_wrapper.context` is the **same object** you passed — `ensure_context_wrapper` (`run_internal/agent_runner_helpers.py:357-363`) does `RunContextWrapper(context=context)` with no copy:

```python
def ensure_context_wrapper(context):
    if isinstance(context, RunContextWrapper):
        return context
    return RunContextWrapper(context=cast(TContext, context))
```

So mutations your tools made are visible both through your own reference and through `result.context_wrapper.context`. You may also pass a pre-built `RunContextWrapper` as `context=` and it is reused by identity.

Use `result.context_wrapper` when you also want SDK runtime metadata — `.usage`, approval state, `.tool_input` (`docs/results.md:228`). Persistence caveat from `docs/context.md:53`: that runtime metadata is saved into a serialized `RunState`, so **don't put secrets in `.context`** if you intend to persist or transmit state.

`ToolContext[T]` (subclass, `agents.tool_context.ToolContext`) additionally exposes `tool_name`, `tool_call_id`, `tool_arguments`, `tool_namespace`, `qualified_tool_name`.

## 7. Streaming gotchas

### Output guardrail tripwire mid-stream

**Exception:** `OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered` (exported from `agents`). **When:** output guardrails run only once the turn reaches `NextStepFinalOutput` — `run.py:1913-1930` shows `await run_output_guardrails(...)` inside `if isinstance(turn_result.next_step, NextStepFinalOutput)`. That is **after** the final message tokens have already been emitted as raw deltas.

**This is the big trap:** you will have already streamed the offending text to your user before the tripwire fires. If you stream raw text deltas straight to a UI, buffer or use a "commit on completion" pattern.

Propagation path: the exception escapes `run_loop_task` → `_check_errors()` (`result.py:1128-1138`) stores it in `_stored_exception` → `stream_events()` raises it at `result.py:1076-1085`, after the `finally` block has drained queues and run cleanup. `docs/guardrails.md:54` confirms: *"Streaming runs use the same persistence ordering as non-streaming runs and raise the terminal exception from `stream_events()`."*

Redaction note (`docs/results.md:224`): when an output guardrail blocks output that came directly from a terminal function tool, `output_guardrail_results` and `tool_output_guardrail_results` are **sanitized** — payloads replaced with `"Output withheld by an output guardrail."`. The sanitized result is on `exc.guardrail_result`.

### Cancellation — yes, `.cancel()` exists

```python
def cancel(self, mode: Literal["immediate", "after_turn"] = "immediate") -> None:
```

(`result.py:878`.) Two modes:
- `"immediate"` (default) — `_cleanup_tasks()` cancels `run_loop_task`, the sandbox-wrapped loop, and both guardrail tasks; sets `is_complete = True`; clears the input-guardrail queue; pushes a `QueueCompleteSentinel` to unblock waiting consumers.
- `"after_turn"` — sets `_cancel_mode` only and returns; the loop stops before the next turn begins. Per the docstring: lets the LLM response finish, executes pending tool calls, saves session state properly, tracks usage accurately.

**Critical:** the docstring says *"After calling cancel(), you should continue consuming stream_events() to allow the cancellation to complete properly."* `docs/results.md:199` repeats this. Breaking out of the `async for` without draining leaves cleanup unfinished.

Also, if the *consuming task itself* is cancelled while awaiting the queue, `stream_events()` catches `asyncio.CancelledError`, calls `self.cancel()`, and re-raises (`result.py:1019-1022`).

### Do exceptions surface from `stream_events()`?

**Yes** — that is the designed channel. The `RunResultStreaming` class docstring: *"The streaming method will raise: A `MaxTurnsExceeded` exception if the agent exceeds the max_turns limit; A tripwire exception if a guardrail is tripped, e.g. `InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered` or `OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered`."* `_check_errors()` also captures failures from `run_loop_task` and `_input_guardrails_task`. Exceptions are raised **after** the generator's `finally` (cleanup, queue drain), so the exception arrives once the run has settled.

**One documented escape hatch / edge case.** A run-loop failure that happens *before* any stream event is produced (the docstring's example: early sandbox initialisation) may not be re-raised through `stream_events()`. Hence `run_loop_exception`, with this exact recipe in its docstring (`result.py:850-876`):

```python
result = Runner.run_streamed(agent, "hello")
async for event in result.stream_events():
    pass
if result.run_loop_exception:
    raise result.run_loop_exception
```

It returns `None` if the loop succeeded, hasn't finished, or was cancelled.

### Other streaming gotchas worth knowing

- **Approvals end the stream early.** If a tool needs approval, `stream_events()` simply *finishes* — no exception. Check `result.interruptions`, then `state = result.to_state()`, `state.approve(interruption)`, and re-run `Runner.run_streamed(agent, state)`. Don't mistake a clean exit for a completed run; check `result.interruptions`.
- **Cancelling during an output guardrail:** `docs/guardrails.md:54` — an immediate `cancel()` while the output guardrail is running cancels the in-flight guardrail and does **not** start a final-turn session write.
- **After `cancel(mode="after_turn")` stopped on a tool turn**, rerun `result.last_agent` with `result.to_input_list(mode="normalized")` to continue the unfinished user turn rather than appending a fresh one (`docs/streaming.md:64`).

## 1. `@function_tool` — exact signature

Source: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/openai-agents-python/v0.22.2/src/agents/tool.py` (lines 2601-2623)

```python
def function_tool(
    func: ToolFunction[...] | None = None,
    *,
    name_override: str | None = None,
    description_override: str | None = None,
    docstring_style: DocstringStyle | None = None,
    use_docstring_info: bool = True,
    failure_error_function: ToolErrorFunction | None | object = _UNSET_FAILURE_ERROR_FUNCTION,
    strict_mode: bool = True,
    is_enabled: bool | Callable[[RunContextWrapper[Any], AgentBase], MaybeAwaitable[bool]] = True,
    needs_approval: bool
    | Callable[[RunContextWrapper[Any], dict[str, Any], str], Awaitable[bool]] = False,
    tool_input_guardrails: list[ToolInputGuardrail[Any]] | None = None,
    tool_output_guardrails: list[ToolOutputGuardrail[Any]] | None = None,
    timeout: float | None = None,
    timeout_behavior: ToolTimeoutBehavior = "error_as_result",
    timeout_error_function: ToolErrorFunction | None = None,
    defer_loading: bool = False,
    custom_data_extractor: FunctionToolCustomDataExtractor | None = None,
    allowed_callers: list[ToolCaller] | None = None,
    output_type: Any | None = None,
    output_json_schema: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> FunctionTool | Callable[[ToolFunction[...]], FunctionTool]:
```

Note the naming asymmetry: the **decorator kwarg is `strict_mode`**, but the **`FunctionTool` field is `strict_json_schema`**; likewise decorator `timeout` → field `timeout_seconds`.

**`@tool` is an official alias.** `src/agents/decorators.py` is literally `tool = function_tool`. The current docs examples use `from agents.decorators import tool`.

**Schema derivation** (`function_schema.py`, and `docs/tools.md` line 505-506):
- Signature via `inspect` + `get_type_hints(func, include_extras=True)`; a Pydantic model is built dynamically (`FuncSchema.params_pydantic_model`), and `params_json_schema` is its `model_json_schema()`.
- Docstrings parsed with griffe. `DocstringStyle = Literal["google", "numpy", "sphinx"]` (`function_schema.py:135`). Auto-detection is a hand-rolled scorer (`_detect_docstring_style`, line 140) because griffe's own auto-detect is an Insiders feature.
- Docstring **text section → tool `description`**; **parameters section → per-argument `description`** in the JSON schema.
- `use_docstring_info=False` skips all docstring parsing (description and arg descriptions both become empty). `description_override` / `name_override` take precedence; `name_override` wins even when docstring info is disabled.
- `Annotated[T, Field(description=...)]` descriptions are merged in, with **docstring winning on conflict** (`param_descs.setdefault(name, description)`, line 385).
- Google-style extra: an `Args:`/`Arguments:`/`Params:`/`Parameters:` section is accepted even without a blank line after the summary (SDK works around a griffe gate).

```python
from agents.decorators import tool  # or: from agents import function_tool

@tool(docstring_style="google")
def read_file(path: str, directory: str | None = None) -> str:
    """Read the contents of a file.

    Args:
        path: The path to the file to read.
        directory: The directory to read the file from.
    """
    return "<file contents>"
```

## 3. `strict_json_schema` / strict mode

- **Default: `True`** — both `strict_mode=True` on the decorator and `FunctionTool.strict_json_schema: bool = True` (`tool.py`), and `FuncSchema.strict_json_schema: bool = True`.
- Enforced in `src/agents/strict_schema.py` via `ensure_strict_json_schema`. What it does/forbids:
  - **Every property becomes required**: `json_schema["required"] = list(properties.keys())` (line 250). So defaults and `Optional` do not make a field omittable — the model must always emit it.
  - **`additionalProperties: False` is forced** on every object (line 236). If a schema already sets `additionalProperties` to anything other than `False`, it raises `UserError` with `_ADDITIONAL_PROPERTIES_ERROR` (line 27-32): *"additionalProperties should not be set for object types… If you really need this, update the function or output tool to not use a strict schema."* This is what makes open `dict[str, X]` arguments fail under strict mode.
  - **Root must not be `anyOf`**: `UserError("The root of a strict JSON schema must not use \`anyOf\`.")` (line 139) — and the root must be a non-nullable object (line 146-150).
  - **`None` defaults are stripped** (line 367).
  - Open objects (no declared properties) rejected with `_OPEN_OBJECT_ERROR`; depth cap `_MAX_SCHEMA_DEPTH = 100`, node cap `_MAX_SCHEMA_NODES = 100_000`.
- **Turning it off:** `@function_tool(strict_mode=False)`. Docstring at `tool.py:2646-2650`: *"If False, it allows non-strict JSON schemas. For example, if a parameter has a default value, it will be optional, additional properties are allowed, etc."* What you lose is the API-side constrained decoding guarantee — the SDK warns *"We **strongly** recommend setting this to True, as it increases the likelihood of correct JSON input."* You then get optional args, unions, and dict types, but the model may emit malformed/incomplete args (surfacing as `ModelBehaviorError`).

## 4. Error handling — `failure_error_function`

Exact name: **`failure_error_function`**. Type alias (`tool.py:204`):

```python
ToolErrorFunction = Callable[[RunContextWrapper[Any], Exception], MaybeAwaitable[str]]
```

Note it is `MaybeAwaitable[str]` — **async error functions are allowed**.

**Default is a sentinel, not the function itself**: `_UNSET_FAILURE_ERROR_FUNCTION = object()` (`tool.py:210`). `resolve_function_tool_failure_error_function` (line 1991) maps the unset sentinel to `default_tool_error_function`. This 3-state design lets the SDK distinguish "unset" from an explicit `None`.

`default_tool_error_function` (`tool.py:1952-1961`), verbatim:

```python
def default_tool_error_function(ctx: RunContextWrapper[Any], error: Exception) -> str:
    """The default tool error function, which just returns a generic error message."""
    json_decode_error = _extract_tool_argument_json_error(error)
    if json_decode_error is not None:
        return (
            "An error occurred while parsing tool arguments. "
            "Please try again with valid JSON. "
            f"Error: {json_decode_error}"
        )
    return f"An error occurred while running the tool. Please try again. Error: {str(error)}"
```

**To make the tool raise instead of returning a string to the model: pass `failure_error_function=None` explicitly.** From `tool.py:2643-2645`: *"If you pass None, then no error message will be sent and instead an Exception will be raised."*

```python
@tool(failure_error_function=None)   # exceptions propagate out of Runner.run
def strict_tool(x: int) -> str: ...
```

One subtlety worth knowing (`docs/tools.md:175`): for a **schema-backed program-owned call** (`allowed_callers` + an output schema), the default failure formatter is *automatically disabled* because free-form text cannot satisfy the output schema — exceptions propagate unless you supply a schema-conforming `failure_error_function`.

## 5. Returning structured output vs a string

Serialization happens in `ItemHelpers.tool_call_output_item` (`src/agents/items.py:845-923`). The resolution order:

1. **`output_type_adapter` set** (you passed `output_type=`): validates, then `json.dumps(dumped, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(",", ":"))`. Mismatch → `UserError("Function tool output does not match its declared output schema.")`.
2. **`output_json_schema` set**: same JSON-object serialization; must be a JSON object or `UserError`.
3. **`isinstance(output, str)`** → passed through unchanged.
4. Programmatic tool calls → structured, else `_JSON_OUTPUT_ADAPTER.dump_json(...)`.
5. **Everything else → `_convert_tool_output(output)`, which is `str(output)`** (`items.py:947-951`).

**This is the key gotcha.** A returned Pydantic model or plain dict does **not** get JSON-serialized by default — it gets `str()`'d. `str(SomeModel(a=1, b="x"))` yields `a=1 b='x'`, and `str({"a": 1})` yields `{'a': 1}` with single quotes (invalid JSON). The only values treated structurally are `ToolOutputText` / `ToolOutputImage` / `ToolOutputFileContent` (or a dict carrying an explicit `"type"` key that validates against them) — `_maybe_get_output_as_structured_function_output`, `items.py:985-1000`.

So to hand the model clean JSON, do one of:

```python
@tool
def get_user(uid: str) -> str:
    return User(name="a", age=3).model_dump_json()   # explicit — recommended

@tool(output_type=User)          # or declare a schema; SDK then JSON-dumps + validates
def get_user2(uid: str) -> User: ...
```

## 6. Async tools

Fully supported. `tool.py:2687` computes `is_sync_function_tool = not inspect.iscoroutinefunction(the_func)`, and at 2730-2739 the invoker awaits coroutines directly while **sync functions are offloaded via `asyncio.to_thread(...)`** — so a blocking sync tool will not stall the event loop, but it does consume a thread-pool slot.

## 7. Tool timeouts — YES, built in (contradicts your premise)

`@function_tool(timeout=<seconds>)`. Implementation is `asyncio.wait_for` inside `_invoke_function_tool_with_metadata` (`tool.py:2224-2228`), so the SDK does exactly what you would have written by hand.

- `timeout_behavior="error_as_result"` (**default**): returns a model-visible message so the model can recover. Default text from `default_tool_timeout_error_message`: `f"Tool '{tool_name}' timed out after {timeout_seconds:g} seconds."`
- `timeout_behavior="raise_exception"`: raises `ToolTimeoutError(tool_name, timeout_seconds)` and fails the run.
- `timeout_error_function=...`: custom message for `error_as_result`.
- `ToolTimeoutBehavior = Literal["error_as_result", "raise_exception"]` (`tool.py:203`).

**Constraint: async handlers only.** `_validate_function_tool_timeout_config` (`tool.py:2865-2887`) raises `ValueError("FunctionTool timeout_seconds is only supported for async @function_tool handlers.")` for sync tools, plus validates the value is finite and `> 0`. Confirmed by `docs/tools.md`: *"Timeout configuration is supported only for async `@function_tool` handlers."*

So: for **sync** tools you still must roll your own (or just make the tool `async`). And `timeout` cancels the task but does not by itself impose an HTTP-level timeout — keep your `httpx` timeouts too.

## 8. `tool_use_behavior` on Agent

`src/agents/agent.py:373-393`, default **`"run_llm_again"`**:

```python

    Literal["run_llm_again", "stop_on_first_tool"] | StopAtTools | ToolsToFinalOutputFunction

```

- `"run_llm_again"` — default; tools run, LLM receives results and responds.

Hosted tools, such as file search, web search, etc. are always processed by the LLM."** Related: `reset_tool_choice: bool = True` (line 395) resets `tool_choice` after a tool call to avoid infinite tool loops.

## 9. `max_turns`

- **Default: `DEFAULT_MAX_TURNS = 10`**, defined in `src/agents/run_config.py:45` (re-exported through `agents.run`). Signature: `max_turns: int | None = DEFAULT_MAX_TURNS` (`run.py:267`, `372`, `474` for `run` / `run_sync` / `run_streamed`).

## 10. Parallel tool calls

**Two independent layers — don't conflate them.**

**Provider side:** `ModelSettings.parallel_tool_calls: bool | None = None` (`src/agents/model_settings.py:114-119`). Default `None` means *defer to the provider*; the docstring notes: *"For most current providers (e.g., OpenAI), this typically means parallel tool calls are enabled (True)."* Set `False` to restrict the model to one tool call per turn.

```python
from agents import Agent, ModelSettings
agent = Agent(name="a", tools=[...], model_settings=ModelSettings(parallel_tool_calls=False))
```

**SDK side:** **Yes, the SDK executes multiple tool calls from one turn concurrently.** In `src/agents/run_internal/tool_execution.py`, `_create_tool_task` (line 1655) wraps each `_run_single_tool` in `asyncio.create_task`, and `_drain_pending_tasks` (1667) uses `asyncio.wait(..., return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED)`.

New in this area: **`max_function_tool_concurrency`** (`run_config.py:139-144`), a cap on concurrent local function tool calls. Default `None` = start all tool calls emitted in a turn. Values `< 1` raise `ValueError("tool_execution.max_function_tool_concurrency must be at least 1")`. Its docstring explicitly notes: *"This does not change provider-side `parallel_tool_calls` behavior."*

## 11. `Agent.tools`, `is_enabled`, `ToolContext`

**`Agent.tools`** — `agent.py:194`: `tools: list[Tool] = field(default_factory=list)`.

**`is_enabled`** — resolved per run in `AgentBase.get_all_tools(run_context)` (`agent.py:272-292`):

```python
async def _check_tool_enabled(tool: Tool) -> bool:
    if not isinstance(tool, FunctionTool):
        return True
    attr = tool.is_enabled
    if isinstance(attr, bool):
        return attr
    res = attr(run_context, self)
    if inspect.isawaitable(res):
        return bool(await res)
    return bool(res)

results = await gather_with_cancel(*(_check_tool_enabled(t) for t in self.tools))
```

Signature `bool | Callable[[RunContextWrapper[Any], AgentBase], MaybeAwaitable[bool]]`, default `True`. Sync **and** async callables both work, and all checks run concurrently. Note it only applies to `FunctionTool` — non-function tools are always enabled. Disabled tools are hidden from the LLM entirely (`tool.py:2651-2653`).

**`ToolContext` exists** — `src/agents/tool_context.py:41-64`, `@dataclass(eq=False) class ToolContext(RunContextWrapper[TContext])`. Fields:

| Field | Type |
|---|---|
| `tool_name` | `str` |
| `tool_call_id` | `str` |
| `tool_arguments` | `str` (raw args string) |
| `tool_call` | `ResponseFunctionToolCall \| None` |
| `tool_namespace` | `str \| None` |
| `agent` | `AgentBase[Any] \| None` |
| `run_config` | `RunConfig \| None` |

It is what `FunctionTool.on_invoke_tool: Callable[[ToolContext[Any], str], Awaitable[Any]]` receives. Because it subclasses `RunContextWrapper`, a tool declaring `RunContextWrapper[T]` as its first param actually receives a `ToolContext` at runtime and can access `.tool_call_id` etc.

- **Tool calls ARE stored.** I ran a tool workflow with a session; `get_items()` returned `['user', 'function_call', 'function_call_output', 'message']`. So tool arguments and tool results persist to disk — relevant if tool I/O is sensitive.
- **Context does grow unboundedly by default.** `SessionSettings(limit=None)` is the default and retrieves *all* items.

### 5. Custom processors

`TracingProcessor` (`src/agents/tracing/processor_interface.py`) is an `abc.ABC` with **six** abstract methods — all must be implemented: `on_trace_start(trace)`, `on_trace_end(trace)`, `on_span_start(span)`, `on_span_end(span)`, `shutdown()`, `force_flush()`.

- `add_trace_processor(p)` — **adds**, so traces still go to OpenAI.
- `set_trace_processors([p])` — **replaces**, so nothing reaches OpenAI. Use this one to stop uploads while keeping local traces.

`span.export()` → `dict[str, Any] | None`; `trace.export()` likewise. Verified span keys: `['ended_at','error','id','object','parent_id','span_data','started_at','trace_id']`. Trace record: `{'object':'trace','id':'trace_...','workflow_name':'W','group_id':'g1','metadata':None}`. Note `group_id` lives on the **trace**, not the span; join spans to traces via `trace_id`.

**Working JSONL processor (executed successfully):**

```python
import json
from agents import TracingProcessor, set_trace_processors

class JsonlTracingProcessor(TracingProcessor):
    def __init__(self, path):
        self._f = open(path, "a", encoding="utf-8"); self._closed = False
    def _write(self, obj):
        if obj is not None and not self._closed:
            self._f.write(json.dumps(obj, default=str) + "\n"); self._f.flush()
    def on_trace_start(self, trace): self._write(trace.export())
    def on_trace_end(self, trace): pass
    def on_span_start(self, span): pass
    def on_span_end(self, span): self._write(span.export())
    def force_flush(self):
        if not self._closed: self._f.flush()
    def shutdown(self):
        if self._closed: return      # MUST be idempotent — atexit calls it too
        self._f.flush(); self._f.close(); self._closed = True

set_trace_processors([JsonlTracingProcessor("spans.jsonl")])
```

Two real bugs I hit and fixed in that sketch, worth keeping: **(a)** a non-idempotent `shutdown()` produces `Error shutting down trace processor` at exit because the global provider's atexit hook calls `shutdown()` again after you do; **(b)** without flushing on write, spans sit in the Python file buffer and a same-process read finds an empty file.

### 6. `trace()` / `custom_span()`

```python
from agents import trace, custom_span

with trace("Joke workflow", group_id="thread_42"):
    await Runner.run(agent, "Tell me a joke")
    with custom_span("my_operation"):
        ...
```

Trace properties: `workflow_name`, `trace_id` (format `trace_<32_alphanumeric>`), `group_id`, `disabled`, `metadata`. Manual form: `t.start(mark_as_current=True)` / `t.finish(reset_current=True)`. Current trace is tracked in a `contextvar`. `flush_traces()` exists for background workers and still flushes buffered data even after tracing is disabled. Default trace name is the literal `"Agent workflow"`.

Real, 572 lines, and it is a full deterministic-test-double guide — **not** a mocking tutorial. ## 1. STREAMING — the big one

**Short answer: streaming is functionally "supported" but is not actually streamed. It is fully buffered on record and replayed as a single chunk. Open-ended streams (SSE) hang on record.**

I verified this from the source in `master`, not by inference from issues. `vcr/stubs/httpx_stubs.py` (172 lines, current master, shared by the `_httpx` and `_httpx2` patchers):

**Record path** (`_vcr_handle_async_request`, lines 119–127):
```python
real_response = await real_handle_async_request(self, real_request)
real_response_content = b"".join([part async for part in real_response.stream])
# Close the original stream so that the connection is released back to the connection pool
with httpx._exceptions.request_context(request=real_response._request):
    await real_response.stream.aclose()
# Reading the response stream consumes the iterator, so we need to restore it
real_response.stream = httpx.ByteStream(real_response_content)
```
The sync twin is lines 144–160. So on **record**, the entire body is drained to memory before your `async with client.stream(...)` block sees anything. There is no incremental pass-through.

**Replay path** (`_deserialize_response`, lines 70–77):
```python
return httpx.Response(
    vcr_response["status"]["code"],
    headers=_deserialize_headers(vcr_response["headers"]),
    # Don't use content, because that closes the response,
    # which we do not want as the real response is unclosed
    stream=httpx.ByteStream(vcr_response["body"]["string"]),
    extensions=extensions,
)
```
`httpx.ByteStream` (verified against `encode/httpx` master `httpx/_content.py`) is:
```python
class ByteStream(AsyncByteStream, SyncByteStream):
    def __init__(self, stream: bytes) -> None:
        self._stream = stream
    def __iter__(self) -> Iterator[bytes]:
        yield self._stream
    async def __aiter__(self) -> AsyncIterator[bytes]:
        yield self._stream
```

Consequences, concretely answering your three questions:

- **Do streamed bodies get consumed/emptied?** Not any more (that was the pre-8.x failure mode — see #832, #884, #895 below). vcrpy now explicitly restores the stream after draining it. Bodies are correct.
- **Do they replay as one chunk instead of incrementally?** **Yes.** `aiter_bytes()` / `iter_bytes()` / `aiter_raw()` yield the whole body in exactly one chunk on replay. Original chunk boundaries and any inter-chunk timing are lost — they are never recorded in the first place. `iter_lines()` still yields correct individual lines (httpx re-splits text regardless of chunking), so line-oriented SSE parsers will produce the right events, but all at once, instantly, with no interleaving.
- **Do they hang?** **Yes, on record, for any stream that does not terminate promptly** — `b"".join([part async for part in real_response.stream])` cannot return until the server closes the connection. This is exactly the reported SSE failure.

The project's own test confirms the weak contract. `tests/integration/test_httpx.py::test_stream` (line 280) only checks the *joined* bytes:
```python
def test_stream(tmpdir, httpbin, do_request):
    url = httpbin.url + "/stream-bytes/512"
    ...
    with vcr.use_cassette(testfile):
        response_content = do_request().stream("GET", url)
        assert len(response_content) == 512
    with vcr.use_cassette(testfile) as cassette:
        cassette_content = do_request().stream("GET", url)
        assert cassette_content == response_content
```
and the helpers do `return b"".join(response.iter_bytes())` (sync, line 59) and `async for c in response.aiter_bytes(): content += c` (async, line 103). **No test asserts chunk count or boundaries.** There is no `text/event-stream` test anywhere in the file (grepped).

Caveat on the changelog wording: the line reads *"Add support for httpx 2.x (#993)"*, which is misleading — it is not a future `httpx` 2.x release, it is **pydantic's `httpx2` fork** (`github.com/pydantic/httpx2`). Issue #990's body names `pydantic/httpx2` and `pydantic/httpx2/tree/main/src/httpcore2` explicitly.

The failure mode before 8.2.0 is worth knowing: **silent bypass.** From `dsfaccini` on #990, 2026-05-28, while migrating pydantic-ai off httpx:

## 4. CONTENT-ENCODING

**Option name: `decode_compressed_response` (boolean kwarg on the `VCR` object / `use_cassette`). Default is `False`.** Added long ago — changelog 1.8.0: `decode_compressed_response option and filter (thanks @jayvdb)` (issue #230).

**Does vcrpy decode before storing?** Only if you opt in. Verified in `vcr/filters.py`:

```python
AVAILABLE_DECOMPRESSORS = {
    "deflate": decompress_deflate,
    "gzip": decompress_gzip,
}
if brotli is not None:
    ...
    AVAILABLE_DECOMPRESSORS["br"] = decompress_brotli
```

Supported: **gzip, deflate, br (brotli)**. **zstd is NOT supported** — no decompressor, and a repo-wide issue search for "zstd" returns **zero results**. A zstd-encoded body is stored as an opaque binary blob (it replays correctly, it's just unreadable/undiffable in the cassette).

Brotli requires one of `brotli`, `brotlipy`, or `brotlicffi` to be installed, and **only became available in 8.1.0** (`#620`). Before that, `Content-Encoding: br` was unsupported — see [#599 "support 'conent-encoding: br'"](https://github.com/kevin1024/vcrpy/issues/599), CLOSED, opened 2021-07-26.

### Caveats

1. **Off by default.** Without it your cassettes contain binary gzip blobs — not reviewable, not greppable, not editable.
2. **Only the first `Content-Encoding` value is examined.** `decode_response` does `decompressor = AVAILABLE_DECOMPRESSORS.get(content_encoding[0])` and silently returns the response undecoded if there's no match. A chained encoding sent as a single header value (`Content-Encoding: br, gzip`) will not match any key and is silently left compressed.
3. **Decompression failures are swallowed.** Each decompressor catches `zlib.error` / `brotli.error` and returns the body unchanged — `# Assume the response was already decompressed`. Changelog 4.4.0: `Bugfix: Make decompression robust towards already decompressed input`. Good for robustness, but it means a genuinely corrupt body is stored as-is with no warning.
4. **It mutates headers.** `decode_response` deletes `content-encoding` and rewrites `content-length` to the decompressed length. Recorded in [#264](https://github.com/kevin1024/vcrpy/issues/264) "decode_compressed_response=True changes the original response header" (CLOSED).
5. **Documented warning**, verbatim from `docs/advanced.rst`:
   > When the ``decode_compressed_response`` keyword argument of a ``VCR`` object is set to True, VCR will decompress "gzip" and "deflate" response bodies before recording. This ensures that these interactions become readable and editable after being serialized.
   >
   > .. note::
   >     Decompression is done before any other specified `Custom Response Filtering`_.
   >
   > This option should be avoided if the actual decompression of response bodies is part of the functionality of the library or app being tested.

   (The docs still say only "gzip" and "deflate" — they were never updated for brotli in 8.1.0.)

## Bottom line for your use

1. **Do not expect incremental streaming.** vcrpy will give you byte-correct streamed bodies, but record buffers fully and replay emits one chunk. If anything under test depends on chunk arrival (progress bars, first-token latency, backpressure, partial-parse behaviour), vcrpy will not exercise it.
2. **SSE / long-lived streams will hang on first record.** #989 is open and unanswered. If your fixtures are SSE, you need to record them some other way, or ensure the endpoint terminates.
3. **If you are on HTTP/2 origins, avoid 8.2.0–8.3.0** until #1029 merges, or apply that patch — #1028 makes vcrpy unable to read its own cassettes. Pinning `vcrpy<8.2` is the reporter's workaround, but that forfeits httpx2.
4. **httpx2 requires >= 8.2.0**, and shares the #1028 bug.
5. **Set `decode_compressed_response=True`** if you want reviewable cassettes; accept that gzip/deflate/br are covered and zstd is not.
